hello.title: Hello, Clojure!
hello.summary: Write your first Clojure program, print text with println, calculate in prefix notation and join text with str.
hello.lesson.0: A Clojure program is a list of expressions. An expression in parentheses is a **function call**: the first item is the function, the other items are its arguments. The function `println` prints its arguments and then ends the line. Text in double quotes, like `"Hello, Clojure!"`, is a **string**.
hello.lesson.2: `println` accepts several arguments and puts a space between them. Numbers are written without quotes. Every `println` starts a new line.
hello.lesson.5: In mathematics you write `1 + 2`. In Clojure the operator comes first, like every other function: `(+ 1 2)`. This is called **prefix notation**. The functions `+` (add), `-` (subtract) and `*` (multiply) accept any number of arguments, so `(+ 1 2 3)` is `6`.
hello.lesson.7: You can put expressions inside other expressions. Clojure first calculates the inner ones. There are no precedence rules to remember: the parentheses show the order.
hello.lesson.10: The function `str` joins all its arguments into one string. Unlike `println`, it adds no spaces, so you write them yourself. Numbers become text, too.
hello.lesson.12: Every opening parenthesis `(` needs a closing one `)`. A missing `)` is the most common error for beginners, so count them when your program does not run.
hello.card.1: `(f a b)`: the function comes first, then the arguments
hello-2.explain: The inner expression comes first: `(- 7 2)` is 5. Then `(* 3 5)` is 15.
hello-3.explain: `str` joins all arguments into one string without spaces.
hello-4.prompt: How do you write 5 + 3 in Clojure?
hello-4.explain: The function always comes first inside the parentheses, and `+` is a function.
hello-5.explain: `println` puts a space between its arguments and ends the line. The second `println` starts a new line.
hello-6.explain: `str` adds no spaces. The code prints `HelloAda`.
hello-7.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 10.
hello-7.explain: `(* 2 5)` multiplies and gives 10. `+` would give 7 and `str` would give `25`.
hello-8.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `Hi, Bo`.
hello-8.explain: `str` joins the two strings. `+` only works with numbers.
hello-9.prompt: Build a line that prints the result of 4 times 5.
hello-9.explain: `(* 4 5)` multiplies, and `println` prints the result. The function always comes first.
hello-10.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `Start`, `6` and `End`.
hello-10.explain: Every `println` prints one line. The calculation `(* 2 (+ 1 2))` is the argument of the second `println`.

values.title: Values
values.summary: Get to know numbers, ratios, strings, keywords, booleans and nil, and give values a name with def.
values.lesson.0: Whole numbers like `42` are **integers**. Numbers with a decimal point, like `3.5`, are **decimal numbers**. When a decimal number takes part in a calculation, the result is a decimal number, too.
values.lesson.2: When you divide two integers with `/` and the result is not whole, Clojure gives a **ratio**: an exact fraction like `7/2`. Nothing is rounded. If you want a decimal result, use a decimal number. `quot` gives the whole part of a division and `mod` gives the rest.
values.lesson.5: `def` gives a value a name. After `(def age 30)`, the name `age` stands for `30`. Names can contain a dash, like `first-name`, and Clojure programmers write them this way.
values.lesson.8: A **keyword** is a name that starts with a colon, like `:red`. It stands for itself, and you use it as a label, for example for the keys of a map (you meet maps in a later unit). The **booleans** `true` and `false` are the answers to yes-or-no questions. `nil` means **no value**.
values.lesson.10: `println` shows a string without quotes. `prn` shows every value the way you write it in code, so strings keep their quotes. This helps you see what a value really is. The function `count` gives the number of characters in a string.
values.lesson.12: Functions whose names end with `?` answer a yes-or-no question with `true` or `false`. For example, `(string? "hi")` and `(nil? nil)` are both `true`, and `(number? "5")` is `false`.
values.card.2: `(def total 12)` gives a value a name
values-1.explain: 9 divided by 3 is exactly 3, so the result is a whole number.
values-2.explain: 6 divided by 4 is not whole, so Clojure gives the ratio `6/4`, shortened to `3/2`.
values-3.explain: 17 divided by 5 is 3 with a rest of 2. `mod` gives the rest.
values-4.explain: `b` is 5 times 2, so 10. Then `(+ a b)` is 5 + 10, which is 15.
values-5.prompt: Which of these is a keyword?
values-5.explain: A keyword starts with a colon. `"size"` is a string and `size` is a name.
values-6.statement: This code prints `"pear"` with the quotes.
values-6.explain: `prn` shows strings the way you write them in code, with quotes. `println` would print `pear`.
values-7.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `2.5`.
values-7.explain: With a decimal number the result is a decimal number: `2.5`. `(/ 5 2)` would give the ratio `5/2`.
values-8.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `Total: 5`.
values-8.explain: The name `total` stands for 5. `"total"` is a string and `:total` is a keyword. `(total)` tries to call 5 as a function.
values-9.prompt: Build a line that gives the name `city` the value `"Rome"`.
values-9.explain: `def` is followed by the name and then the value. Clojure needs no `=`.
values-10.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `Area: 12`.
values-10.explain: A name must exist before you use it: `height` needs `width`, and `area` needs both.
values-11.prompt: Match the value with its kind.
values-12.explain: `def` takes a name and a value, without `=`. The line must be `(def people 700000)`.
functions.title: Functions
functions.summary: Write your own functions with defn and fn, use the short form #(...), and accept different numbers of arguments.
functions.lesson.0: `defn` defines a function. After `defn` come the name, the **parameters** in square brackets and the body. A function returns the value of its last expression. Clojure has no `return` keyword.
functions.lesson.2: A function can have several parameters. You call your own functions the same way as the built-in ones.
functions.lesson.4: The body can contain several expressions. All of them run in order, but only the value of the last one is returned.
functions.lesson.7: `fn` creates a function without a name, an **anonymous function**. You can give it a name with `def` or call it directly. The short form `#(...)` is even shorter: inside it, `%` is the argument. With several arguments you write `%1`, `%2` and so on.
functions.lesson.10: The number of arguments a function takes is its **arity**. One function can have several arities. Each version gets its own parentheses with its parameters and body. One version can call another one, for example to fill in a default value.
functions.lesson.12: If you call a function with a number of arguments it does not accept, the program stops with an error that says `Wrong number of args`.
functions.lesson.13: Function names use lowercase words joined with dashes, like `total-price`. Choose names that say what the function returns or does.
functions.card.0: `(defn square [x] (* x x))` defines a function
functions.card.1: The last expression is the return value
functions.card.2: `(fn [x] (* 2 x))` is a function without a name
functions.card.3: `#(* 2 %)` is the short form, `%1 %2` for more arguments
functions-1.explain: `triple` multiplies its argument by 3, and 3 times 7 is 21.
functions-2.explain: The arguments go to the parameters in order: `a` is 3 and `b` is 10, so 3 - 10 is -7.
functions-3.explain: `%` is 9, and 9 divided by 2 is the ratio `9/2`.
functions-4.explain: Calling `info` first prints `x is 2`. Then it returns 3, the value of its last expression, and the outer `println` prints it.
functions-5.prompt: Which function does the same as `#(+ % 10)`?
functions-5.explain: `fn` needs its parameters in square brackets, and the call `(+ x 10)` needs its own parentheses. `defn` needs a name.
functions-6.explain: `greet` is called without arguments, so the version with `[]` runs and returns `Hello!`.
functions-7.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 27.
functions-7.explain: `defn` defines a named function. `def` only names a value, and `fn` creates a function without giving it a name you can use later.
functions-8.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 15.
functions-8.explain: In the short form `#(...)`, the argument is called `%`.
functions-9.prompt: Build a function `add-two` that adds 2 to its argument.
functions-9.explain: `defn`, then the name, then the parameters in square brackets, then the body. The body's value is returned without `return`.

functions-10.explain: The function needs both arities: with one argument it calls itself with two. The line with `)))` closes the whole `defn`, so it comes last in the function.

functions-12.explain: Parameters go into square brackets: `(defn square [x]`.
conditions.title: Decisions
conditions.summary: Compare values, choose between results with if, when and cond, and combine conditions with and, or and not.
conditions.lesson.0: Comparisons are functions, too. `=` checks if values are equal, `not=` checks if they are different, and `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=` compare numbers. They return `true` or `false`. `(< 1 2 3)` checks if the numbers go up from left to right.
conditions.lesson.2: `if` takes three parts: a condition, the value when the condition is true, and the value when it is false. `if` is an expression, so it returns a value that you can print or use.
conditions.lesson.4: Only `false` and `nil` count as false. Every other value counts as true, even `0` and the empty string `""`.
conditions.lesson.7: `when` has only one branch, and it can contain several expressions. They all run when the condition is true. When the condition is false, nothing runs and `when` returns `nil`.
conditions.lesson.9: `cond` takes pairs of a test and a result. It returns the result of the first test that is true and ignores the rest. The keyword `:else` as the last test always counts as true, so it catches all other cases.
conditions.lesson.11: `and` is true when all its conditions are true. `or` is true when at least one is true. `not` turns `true` into `false` and `false` into `true`.
conditions.lesson.13: In Clojure, `=` only compares. It never changes a value. You give names to values with `def`.
conditions.card.1: `(if test "yes" "no")` returns one of two values
conditions.card.2: `(when test ...)` runs several expressions or returns `nil`
conditions-1.explain: 7 is not greater than 10, so `if` returns the third part, `small`.
conditions-2.explain: The first test `(< 0 0)` is false. The second test `(= 0 0)` is true, so `cond` returns `zero`.
conditions-3.explain: `(< 1 2)` is true but `(> 1 2)` is false. `and` needs all conditions to be true.
conditions-4.explain: Only `false` and `nil` count as false. The empty string counts as true.
conditions-5.explain: `cond` returns the result of the first true test. `(> 15 10)` is true, so the later tests are not checked.
conditions-6.explain: `=` accepts more than two arguments and is true when all of them are equal.
conditions-7.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `adult adult child`.
conditions-7.explain: 18 must count as adult, too, so you need "greater than or equal": `>=`.
conditions-8.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `true`.
conditions-8.explain: `(> 3 1)` is true and `(< 3 1)` is false. `or` needs only one true condition.
conditions-9.prompt: Build an expression that gives `"yes"` when `n` is less than 0 and `"no"` otherwise.
conditions-9.explain: `if` takes the condition, then the value for true, then the value for false. Clojure needs no `then` or `else`.
conditions-10.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `Fizz FizzBuzz 7`.
conditions-10.explain: `cond` uses the first true test, so the test for 15 must come before the test for 3. `:else` comes last.

conditions-11.pairs.2: a is less than or equal to b
conditions-11.pairs.3: turns true into false and false into true

conditions-12.explain: `if` takes exactly one expression for true and one for false. To run several expressions, use `(when (> score 50)`.
collections.title: Collections
collections.summary: Keep many values in vectors, lists, maps and sets, and read and add elements with get, count and conj.
collections.lesson.0: A **vector** keeps values in order, written in square brackets: `[1 2 3]`. `count` gives the number of elements and `first` the first one. `get` gives the element at an index. The index starts at `0`, and an index that does not exist gives `nil`.
collections.lesson.2: `conj` adds an element. For a vector it adds it at the end. Clojure collections never change: `conj` returns a new vector, and the old one stays the same. This is called **immutability**.
collections.lesson.4: A **list** is written in parentheses. But in code, parentheses mean a function call, so you put a quote `'` in front of a list of data: `'(1 2 3)`. `conj` adds to the front of a list.
collections.lesson.7: A **map** stores pairs of a key and a value in curly braces. The keys are often keywords. `get` looks up the value for a key, and a keyword can also look itself up: `(:age person)`. A missing key gives `nil`, or the default value you pass to `get` as third argument. Commas count as spaces, and Clojure prints them between the pairs.
collections.lesson.10: A **set** contains every value at most once and is written `#{...}`. `contains?` checks if a value is in the set. Adding a value that is already there changes nothing.
collections.lesson.12: Sets and large maps have no fixed order. Do not rely on the order in which their elements are printed.
collections-1.explain: The index starts at 0, so index 2 is the third element, 30.
collections-2.explain: The keyword `:ben` looks up its value in the map, which is 5.
collections-3.explain: `conj` adds to the front of a list. For a vector it would add at the end.
collections-4.explain: A set contains every value at most once. 2 is already in it, so the set still has 3 elements.
collections-5.explain: `conj` returns a new vector and does not change `nums`. The code prints `[1 2 3]`.
collections-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `Bo`.
collections-6.explain: `(get user :name)` looks up the value for the key `:name`. `contains?` would only print `true`.
collections-7.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `[a b c]`.
collections-7.explain: Only a vector prints with square brackets, and `conj` adds to its end. A list would get `"c"` at the front.
collections-8.prompt: Build an expression that looks up `:price` in `item` and gives `0` when the key is missing.
collections-8.explain: `get` takes the map, the key and, as third argument, a default value.

collections-9.explain: `basket` must exist before `conj` can use it. `conj` returns a new vector, so `basket` still has 1 element.

collections-12.explain: Every key in a map needs a value, for example `(def point {:x 3 :y 4})`.
sequences.title: Sequences
sequences.summary: Process collections step by step with map, filter and reduce, create numbers with range, and chain steps with ->>.
sequences.lesson.0: `range` creates numbers. `(range 5)` gives the numbers from `0` to `4`, and `(range 1 6)` the numbers from `1` to `5`: the end is not included. A third argument sets the step. The result is a **sequence**, which prints in parentheses like a list.
sequences.lesson.2: `map` calls a function on every element and returns a new sequence with the results. The function `inc` adds 1 to a number. You can pass any function to `map`: a built-in one, your own or a `#(...)`.
sequences.lesson.4: `filter` keeps the elements for which the function returns true. The functions `even?` and `odd?` check if a number is even or odd.
sequences.lesson.6: `reduce` combines all elements into one value with a function of two arguments. `(reduce + [1 2 3 4])` calculates `1 + 2`, then adds `3`, then `4`. You can also pass a start value before the collection.
sequences.lesson.8: `take` gives the first elements of a sequence. `(range)` without arguments never ends, but that is no problem: Clojure sequences are **lazy**, which means an element is only calculated when it is needed.
sequences.lesson.11: Nested calls are read from the inside out. The macro `->>` lets you write the steps from top to bottom instead: it puts the result of each step as the **last** argument into the next step.
sequences.lesson.13: The example above does the same as `(reduce + (map #(* % %) (filter odd? (range 1 11))))`. With `->>` you can read the steps in the order they happen.
sequences.card.2: `(filter even? xs)` keeps the even numbers
sequences-1.explain: `map` multiplies every element by 10 and returns a sequence, printed in parentheses.
sequences-3.explain: `filter` keeps the elements for which `odd?` is true. `map` would give the list of booleans.
sequences-4.explain: `range` starts at the first number and stops before the second one.
sequences-5.statement: This code never ends, because `(range)` never ends.
sequences-5.explain: Sequences are lazy. `take` asks only for 3 elements, so the code prints `(0 1 2)`.
sequences-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `(3 5)`.
sequences-6.explain: `filter` keeps 2 and 4, and `map inc` turns them into 3 and 5.
sequences-7.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 24.
sequences-7.explain: 2 times 3 times 4 is 24. With `+` the result would be 9.
sequences-8.prompt: Build an expression that gives the first 3 even numbers.
sequences-8.explain: `filter` keeps the even numbers of the endless `(range)`, and `take` stops after 3 of them.
sequences-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints 24.
sequences-9.explain: First the numbers 1 to 5 are doubled to 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10. Then `filter` keeps 6, 8 and 10, and their sum is 24.
sequences-10.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.

sequences-12.explain: The end of `range` is not included. To get 1 to 5 you need `(def nums (range 1 6))`.
recursion.title: Local names and recursion
recursion.summary: Give values local names with let, write functions that call themselves, and repeat steps with loop and recur.
recursion.lesson.0: `let` gives values names that exist only inside the `let`. First comes a vector with pairs of names and values, then the body. A later name can use the earlier ones. The `let` returns the value of its last expression.
recursion.lesson.2: A name from `let` is not visible outside. Inside the `let`, it hides a name from `def` with the same name, but the `def` value does not change.
recursion.lesson.5: A function can call itself. This is called **recursion**. It needs a **base case**, where it stops calling itself. The function `dec` subtracts 1 from a number. The **factorial** of 5 is 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1.
recursion.lesson.7: Each call waits for the result of the next call. Every waiting call needs memory, so with many thousands of calls the program stops with a `StackOverflowError`.
recursion.lesson.9: `loop` sets starting values, like `let`. `recur` jumps back to the start of the `loop` with new values. It needs no extra memory, so it can repeat millions of times. `recur` must be the last step of the loop: nothing may run after it.
recursion.lesson.11: A loop often carries a result along, like `total` here. When the loop stops calling `recur`, it returns the value of its last expression.
recursion.lesson.13: `recur` also works without `loop`: then it jumps back to the start of the function. In everyday code you often use `map`, `filter` and `reduce` instead of writing loops yourself.
recursion.card.0: `(let [a 1 b (+ a 1)] (* a b))` local names
recursion.card.1: Recursion: a function calls itself and needs a base case
recursion-1.explain: `a` is 3 and `b` is 3 + 4, so 7. Then 3 times 7 is 21.
recursion-2.explain: The calls add 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 0. The base case `(= n 0)` returns 0, and the sum is 10.
recursion-3.explain: Inside the `let`, `x` is 2, so the first line is 3. Outside, `x` is still 5.
recursion-4.explain: The loop adds the squares of 0, 1 and 2. When `i` is 3, it prints the vector and stops.
recursion-5.explain: `total` exists only inside the `let`. The last line cannot use it, so the program stops with an error.
recursion-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 24.
recursion-6.explain: The function calls itself. `recur` does not work here, because the multiplication still runs after the call.
recursion-7.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 5, 3 and 1.
recursion-7.explain: `(- i 2)` makes `i` smaller by 2 in each round: 5, 3, 1. Then `i` is -1 and the loop stops.
recursion-8.prompt: Build a `let` that names `a` 4 and `b` 5 and multiplies them.
recursion-8.explain: The names and values go into one vector, without `=`. The body comes after the vector.
recursion-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints 32.
recursion-9.explain: The loop starts with `i` 0 and `result` 1. Until `i` reaches `n`, `recur` multiplies the result by `base`. 2 to the power of 5 is 32.
recursion-10.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
recursion-11.explain: The names of a `let` go into a vector: `(let [half (/ n 2)]`.
recursion-12.explain: `n` never gets smaller, so the base case is never reached and the program stops with a `StackOverflowError`. Fix: `(factorial (dec n))`.
maps.title: Working with maps
maps.summary: Change maps with assoc, dissoc and update, read keys and values, chain steps with -> and take values out with destructuring.
maps.lesson.0: `assoc` returns a new map with a key added or changed. `dissoc` returns a new map without a key. Like all Clojure collections, the original map never changes.
maps.lesson.2: `update` changes a value with a function. `(update m :k f)` calls `f` with the old value and stores the result. Extra arguments go to the function after the old value.
maps.lesson.4: `keys` gives all keys of a map and `vals` all values. Small maps keep the order in which you wrote them, but in general a map has no fixed order.
maps.lesson.7: The macro `->` works like `->>`, but it puts each result as the **first** argument into the next step. This fits maps well, because `assoc`, `dissoc` and `update` take the map as their first argument.
maps.lesson.10: **Destructuring** takes values out of a collection right where you name them, in a `let` or in the parameters of a function. A vector like `[x y]` takes elements by position. A map like `{:keys [city zip]}` takes the values of the keys `:city` and `:zip`.
maps.lesson.12: A key that is missing from the map gives `nil` in destructuring. As a rule of thumb, use `->` for maps and `->>` for sequences.
maps.card.0: `(assoc m :k v)` adds or changes, `(dissoc m :k)` removes
maps.card.1: `(update m :score inc)` changes a value with a function
maps.card.4: `(let [{:keys [a b]} m] ...)` and `[[x y] v]` destructure
